summary:
TerraScope is a web-based platform that brings NASA satellite fire and heat detections together in one place, so people can explore and understand them. Our first demonstration area is the Kurdistan Region of Iraq.

NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS sensors observe heat activity differently. They have different resolutions, sensitivities, and observation times, so their data are hard to compare. TerraScope collects both, analyzes historical patterns, compares the sensors while showing reliability and uncertainty, and highlights periods that differ from the norm. It also estimates where hotspot detections may recur over the next 3, 7, or 14 days. Users can explore results through interactive maps, a 3D globe, charts, an AI assistant, and plain-language reports.

This matters because satellite data are only useful when people can understand them. TerraScope makes this information accessible to researchers, students, and analysts. It is a developed prototype. Its analysis components have been tested with simulated data, and real-world validation is ongoing. A hotspot is a heat detection, not necessarily a wildfire.
details:
TerraScope: Project Details

What does it do, and how does it work?

NASA satellites watch the Earth and find places with heat. These places are called “hotspots.” TerraScope collects this information and puts it in one website.

It works in five easy steps:

  1. NASA satellites see heat on Earth.
  2. TerraScope collects the information and organizes it.
  3. It studies the past data and compares two satellite types (MODIS and VIIRS).
  4. It finds unusual activity. It also estimates where hotspots may appear again.
  5. You explore the results with maps, a 3D globe, charts, an AI assistant, and reports.

TerraScope has these main features:

  • Fire Memory: shows yearly, monthly, and seasonal history.
  • Satellite Harmonization: compares MODIS and VIIRS, and shows how sure we are.
  • Anomaly Detection: finds times when activity is different from normal.
  • Hotspot Forecasting: estimates where hotspots may appear again in 3, 7, or 14 days.
  • Interactive Exploration: maps and a 3D Earth globe.
  • AI Assistant and Reports: ask questions and get reports in simple language.

What are the benefits?

  • Satellite data becomes easy to understand, even for people with no technical background.
  • MODIS and VIIRS are in one place, so you do not need to compare them yourself.
  • Researchers, students, and analysts can study the past and see changes.

What is the intended impact?

We want to make satellite information easier to use, understand, and explore. We want people to understand their region better, so they can make better decisions about the future.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software did you use?

I do not have this information in your project document, and I do not want to invent it. Please fill this in with your team:

  • Programming languages: python, javascript
  • Web tools or frameworks: HTML,CSS,REACT JS, FastApi
  • NASA data source: FIRMS API and  MAP_KEY
  • AI assistant tools: Claude AI, Chat gpt, Gemeni, Antigravity, AiStudio
  • Hardware: Runs on Laptop

How is it creative?

  • It puts two different satellite views into one story, instead of showing them separately.
  • It shows uncertainty openly, so users know how much to trust each result.
  • It is a platform for exploring, with a 3D globe and an AI assistant, and not only a map.
  • It explains complex science in simple words.

What did your team consider?

We thought carefully about the limits of the data:

  • Different satellites do not see the Earth in the same way.
  • A hotspot is a heat detection. It is not always a wildfire.
  • Farming fires and factories can also make heat.
  • Missing data does not mean zero activity.
  • Predictions and comparisons always have uncertainty.

We also were honest about the project’s status. TerraScope is a developed prototype. Its main analysis parts were tested with simulated data. We still need to check how well it works with real data. We do not say that TerraScope confirms wildfires, or predicts when fires start or how they spread.
